title: Women's and Environmental Movements

cards.h: Two movements that changed what politics means
cards.b:
The women's movement and the environmental movement widened Indian politics beyond class and caste. They asked who does unpaid work, who controls forests and rivers, and whose "development" counts.

Both produced laws, judgments and new ideas such as ecofeminism and the "environmentalism of the poor". UPSC asks about their phases, key cases and debates.

• Reform era: social reformers on sati, widow remarriage and education; women in the freedom struggle.
  • Towards Equality (1974): report of the Committee on the Status of Women in India, with Vina Mazumdar as member-secretary, showed women's position had worsened in many respects. It sparked women's studies.
  • Autonomous women's groups from the late 1970s: campaigns on dowry deaths, rape, sati and domestic violence.
  • Mathura case (Tukaram v. State of Maharashtra, 1979): an open letter by four law professors led to the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1983.

• Roop Kanwar sati (Deorala, 1987) led to the Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act, 1987.
  • Shah Bano (1985) and the 1986 Act raised the question of personal law and women's rights.
  • Bhanwari Devi (1992), a sathin gang-raped for stopping a child marriage, led to Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) guidelines and the POSH Act, 2013.
  • Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.
  • Nirbhaya (December 2012) led to the Justice J.S. Verma Committee and the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013.
  • Shayara Bano (2017) on triple talaq; Joseph Shine (2018) on adultery; Sabarimala (2018).
  • Women's reservation: one-third in local bodies (1992); the 106th Amendment (2023), notified on 16 April 2026, awaits delimitation.

Radha Kumar, The History of Doing (1993)

An illustrated history of women's movements and campaigns in India from 1800 to 1990.

Uma Chakravarti, Gendering Caste (2003)

Caste and gender are linked: control over women's sexuality maintains caste purity ("Brahmanical patriarchy").

Gopal Guru, "Dalit Women Talk Differently" (1995)

Dalit women face both caste and patriarchy; mainstream feminism and Dalit politics both overlooked them.

Nivedita Menon, Seeing Like a Feminist (2012)

Shows how patriarchy shapes everyday life, from family to law.

• Bishnoi sacrifice (Khejarli, 1730): Amrita Devi and others died protecting trees; an early symbol.
  • Chipko (from 1973, Chamoli in Uttarakhand): villagers hugged trees to stop commercial felling. Gaura Devi led the women of Reni in 1974. Leaders included Chandi Prasad Bhatt and Sunderlal Bahuguna. It led to a 15-year ban on green felling in the Himalayan forests of Uttar Pradesh (1980).
  • Appiko (Karnataka, 1983): Chipko's southern counterpart.
  • Silent Valley (Kerala, 1970s-80s): campaign by KSSP and others stopped a hydroelectric dam; declared a national park in 1984.
  • Narmada Bachao Andolan (from 1985, Medha Patkar, Baba Amte) against displacement by Sardar Sarovar. In NBA v. Union of India (2000), the Supreme Court allowed construction to continue. The World Bank withdrew in 1993.
  • Plachimada (Kerala, 2002): villagers against a Coca-Cola plant over groundwater.
  • Niyamgiri (Odisha, 2013): Gram Sabhas rejected bauxite mining.

Ramachandra Guha, The Unquiet Woods (1989)

Chipko as a peasant movement rooted in resistance to state forestry, not just ecology.

Madhav Gadgil and Ramachandra Guha, This Fissured Land (1992)

An ecological history of India showing how colonial and post-colonial forest policy hurt local communities.

Guha and Joan Martinez-Alier, Varieties of Environmentalism (1997)

The environmentalism of the poor: in the South, struggles are about survival and livelihood, unlike Northern concerns with wilderness.

Vandana Shiva, Staying Alive (1988)

Ecofeminism: women and nature are both exploited by "maldevelopment".

Bina Agarwal, "The Gender and Environment Debate" (1992)

Feminist environmentalism: women's link to nature comes from their material role and work, not from essence.

Achievements: laws (POSH, domestic violence, Forest Rights Act 2006, Environment Protection Act 1986), institutions (NCW, National Green Tribunal 2010) and public awareness.

Limits:

  • Women's movement criticised as urban, upper-caste and middle class; Dalit and Muslim women raise separate voices.
  • Laws often poorly implemented (conviction rates, ICCs under POSH).
  • Environmental movements struggle against the growth agenda; dams and mines largely go ahead.
  • Charges of being "anti-development" and restrictions on NGOs under FCRA.

• M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024): a right against the adverse effects of climate change.
  • Joshimath land subsidence (2023) and Himalayan projects.
  • Hasdeo Aranya and Great Nicobar projects.
  • Wrestlers' protest (2023) against the then federation chief over sexual harassment allegations.
  • R.G. Kar case (Kolkata, August 2024) and protests on doctors' and women's safety.
  • Women's reservation: the 106th Amendment in force from 16 April 2026, but the 131st Amendment Bill to speed delimitation was defeated on 17 April 2026.

"Trace the evolution of the women's movement in India."
"Environmental movements in India are movements of the poor." Discuss.
"Compare ecofeminism and feminist environmentalism."

Structure: phases and campaigns of the women's movement with laws; feminist thinkers including Dalit feminism; environmental movements (Chipko, NBA, Silent Valley); thinkers (Guha, Shiva, Agarwal); achievements and limits; recent cases.
